title: Loose Parts Maths
strapline: Conkers in tens-frames, pebbles on number tracks, buttons shared fairly — number you can hold, move and rearrange.
intent: Children count with one-to-one correspondence, moving a real object for each number word.
Children compose and decompose small numbers — five pebbles split into two and three and back again.
Children subitise, sort and pattern with countable, moveable, appealing materials.
Children compare and measure through their hands — more, fewer, longer, heavier, enough.
Children solve genuine problems — fair shares, one each, how many more do we need.
implementation: Stock countable loose parts worth counting — conkers, gems, buttons, shells — in generous quantities.
Provide frames, tracks and sorting rings — five-frames, tens-frames, number tracks, hoops — as quiet invitations, not drills.
Count aloud with a touch per object and make a fuss of the last number: 'one, two, three — THREE conkers!'
Make deliberate errors for children to catch — count one twice, skip one, declare the wrong total.
Explore composing numbers: 'five gems — how many ways can we split them between the two bowls?'
Set real problems with the parts — share the buttons fairly, put one bead in each cup, fill the frame.
Let children invent their own sorting and pattern rules and explain them back to you.
key_questions: How many do you think there are — shall we check?
How many ways can you split these five between the two bowls?
Have we got enough for everyone to have one — how could we find out?
Which pile has more? How do you know?
What's your rule for putting those ones together?

impact.text: Children count moveable objects with one-to-one correspondence and know the last number is the answer.
Children subitise small amounts on frames and in handfuls without counting.
Children compose and decompose small numbers, splitting and recombining a set.
Children sort, match and pattern by their own rules and explain them.
Children compare amounts and sizes using words like more, fewer, longer and heavier.
Children reach for the loose parts to solve real problems — sharing fairly, one in each cup.

enhancements: Generous collections of conkers, gems, buttons and shells.
Five-frames, tens-frames and number tracks to fill.
Sorting rings, muffin tins and bowls for grouping and one-in-each.
Balance scales and natural treasures for comparing weight.
Numeral cards and dice to match to quantities.
A 'how many ways' splitting mat with two bowls.
Mystery-bag estimates: grab a handful, guess, then count.

playing_exploring: Children handle beautiful countable things because they want to — the maths follows the fascination.
Open collections invite children to invent their own counting and sorting games.
active_learning: Checking a guess by counting, and being right, is a satisfaction children chase again.
Children persist to fill the frame or share the set exactly.
creating_thinking: Children spot patterns and use them to predict what comes next.
They find their own strategies — grouping, lining up, splitting — and can say what worked.
